pitch.title: Come Over to My House Tomorrow
pitch.brief: Central figure: Steve Jobs, acting for Apple, wants the Siri assistant. In February 2010 Siri Inc. (CEO Dag Kittlaus, with Adam Cheyer and Tom Gruber, spun out of SRI's DARPA-funded CALO project) had just put its app in the App Store. About two weeks later Jobs phoned Kittlaus's office unannounced and told him to come to his house the next day. Opposition: the founders, who had just raised money, had a good launch and had distribution deals planned, and who turned him down at once. Story question: will the team sell? The expected answer is no. The turn is that within weeks, in April 2010, they sold for a reported $200M, after Jobs persuaded them that Siri would be core to Apple and not a minor feature. The episode ends at the sale. The scene is the cold call and the house visit. It shows Apple reaching its AI assistant by buying it, and a government-funded AI project becoming a product. Caveats: this is closer to a `deal` than a pure founding moment. The sources are retellings, mostly Cheyer's own account, and reporting should look for Kittlaus's and Gruber's versions.

draft.title: The Founders Who Told Steve Jobs No

hook.on_screen: Siri's founders told Steve Jobs no

rungs.purpose: The hook: a startup refused Steve Jobs and Apple still ended up owning Siri. The viewer should want to know how.

lines.text: The founders of Siri turned Steve Jobs down flat, and weeks later Apple owned Siri.

rungs.purpose: Set the scene: what Siri was in early 2010, and that it came from government-funded research. The viewer learns what Jobs was after.

lines.text: Back then, Siri was a brand-new free iPhone app, a personal assistant in your pocket, spun out of a government-funded AI project at SRI.

rungs.purpose: Motive before action: Jobs wants Siri, and we meet its CEO, the man he goes after.

lines.text: Steve Jobs wanted it, and Siri's CEO, Dag Kittlaus, later said Jobs felt "we cracked it."

rungs.purpose: The cold call: Jobs phones Kittlaus himself. We meet the source of this account, and it should feel surreal and personal.

lines.text: Weeks after the launch, Jobs phoned Kittlaus himself, and co-founder Adam Cheyer recalls him saying, "Hey, it's Steve, come over to my house tomorrow."

rungs.purpose: Jobs's pressure in action: Kittlaus has plans, and Jobs simply works around them. A small, funny moment.

lines.text: Kittlaus said he couldn't, because he was taking his wife to the ballet.
Jobs answered, "Really? Well you could come over before."

rungs.purpose: The house visit: three hours by the fireplace, and Jobs says what he wants. The viewer waits for the answer.

lines.text: So Kittlaus went, and sat with Jobs for about three hours in front of his fireplace.
Jobs made clear he wanted to buy Siri.

rungs.purpose: The peak: the founders refuse Steve Jobs to his face and name their condition. Their defiance should feel real.

lines.text: The founders turned him down "with no hesitation," and Cheyer told Jobs, "If it's going to be a feature hidden away, then we're not interested."

rungs.purpose: The turn: Jobs keeps pushing and meets their exact condition. The viewer sees how the no became a yes.

lines.text: Jobs kept at it, and over several more talks he convinced them Siri wouldn't be "a tiny feature" but "something core to Apple's strategy."

rungs.purpose: The sale: the no becomes a deal, and the hook's promise is paid.

lines.text: In April 2010, Apple bought Siri, for a price press reports put at about 200 million dollars.

rungs.purpose: The landing: Siri reaches the iPhone just before Jobs dies. It should feel bittersweet.

lines.text: Siri reached the iPhone in October 2011, announced the day before Jobs died.

draft.close_question: Should Siri's founders have kept saying no?

The founders' immediate refusal and Jobs's 'core, not a feature' persuasion rest on Cheyer's account alone, in two tellings, and the exact date of the call is disputed (two weeks to about March 2010).

pitch.title: The Intern Who Took Redmond's Recipe to Google
pitch.brief: Summer 2011, Mountain View. Microsoft had the head start in deep-learning speech. Li Deng invited Geoffrey Hinton to Redmond in 2009, and Hinton's student George Dahl then trained a network on Bing voice-search data that beat anything else in development there. Hinton's other student, Navdeep Jaitly, took the same approach to Google as a PhD intern from June to August 2011, under manager Vincent Vanhoucke. Google's Android speech service was stuck at about 23 percent error in Metz's account. Jaitly's CV says he cut the word error rate of Google's best voice-search system from 16.0 to 11.8 percent. Google put deep learning in Android 4.1 in 2012, calling it its answer to Siri. Fortune reports Microsoft shipped it first, in 2011. Tension: a rival's lab gets the winning method through the same professor, who publishes openly. Focus on Jaitly's internship and the race to ship, with Deng's view from Microsoft. Verify who shipped first and how Microsoft saw it; the rivalry is implied by the record, not stated.

draft.title: One Professor, Two Rivals: The Intern Who Brought Deep Speech to Google

hook.on_screen: Microsoft got it first. A Google intern followed.

rungs.purpose: Hook: open on the race. Microsoft held the speech breakthrough first, then a summer intern brought it to Google, so the viewer asks how.

lines.text: Microsoft got the trick that taught phones to understand speech first, and then a summer intern carried the very same trick into Google.

rungs.purpose: Introduce the source of the trick. Hinton, who the viewer knows as a Nobel winner, was then a professor betting on deep neural networks.

lines.text: That trick came from Geoffrey Hinton, a Toronto professor years before his Nobel Prize, who bet on deep neural networks.

rungs.purpose: Microsoft moves first. Its researcher brings Hinton in, which opens the head start.

rungs.purpose: The head start becomes real. Hinton's student makes the method work on Microsoft's Bing voice data.

lines.text: Microsoft Research says that by August 2010, Hinton's student George Dahl, working with Deng, had it running on Bing voice-search data.

rungs.purpose: The turn. The results are public, and a second Hinton student walks into Microsoft's rival with the same method.

lines.text: Those results were published in May 2011, and that June another Hinton student, Navdeep Jaitly, arrived at Google to try it there.

rungs.purpose: Peak: in one summer, the intern's network beats Google's best system by a wide margin.

lines.text: On Google's voice-search test, the old system got 16 words in every hundred wrong.
Jaitly's network cut that to 12.3.

rungs.purpose: Google's own speech researcher admits nobody expected it, which shows how big the jump was.

lines.text: Google's Vincent Vanhoucke later said, "It kind of came as a surprise that we could do so much better by just changing the model."

rungs.purpose: Google ships it to Android phones, and the gain reaches millions of users.

lines.text: In 2012, Google put a deep neural network into Android voice search, and Vanhoucke said it cut wrong words by 20 to 25 percent.

rungs.purpose: The race result: Microsoft's executive says Microsoft shipped first, so the head start counted.

lines.text: But Microsoft's Peter Lee told Fortune that Microsoft had put it into its products in 2011, before Google followed in August 2012.

rungs.purpose: Twist: the rivals publish the method together, openly.

lines.text: In November 2012, researchers from Toronto, Microsoft, Google and IBM published one open review together, in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine.

rungs.purpose: Landing: the professor, his two students and both rival companies' researchers appear on one author list.

pitch.title: The $34.5 Billion Offer for a Browser Nobody Was Selling
pitch.brief: Central figure: Aravind Srinivas, Perplexity's CEO, who wants a browser of his own that reaches hundreds of millions of people, so his answer engine no longer depends on someone else's front door. On 12 August 2025, with a federal judge weighing whether Google must sell Chrome to end its search monopoly, Perplexity sent an unsolicited $34.5 billion offer for it (WSJ, Verge). The sum was well above Perplexity's own valuation, which was reportedly about $14–20 billion that summer. Opposition: Google, which did not want to sell and was arguing against divestiture, and the judge who would decide the remedy. Story question: does a startup's public bid change what a court and a rival do with Chrome? The episode runs from the bid to the judge's remedy ruling in early September 2025 (verify the date). The turn must be reported. My working guess is that the offer was a bet on being the buyer if the ruling went one way, and that the ruling made it moot. Source limits: I could not open the WSJ or Verge pieces this session. Only the Wikipedia summaries were read, so the funding, the pledges and the ruling all need verification. The whole pitch rests on those details.

draft.title: The $34.5 Billion Bid Nobody Mentioned

hook.on_screen: A startup bid $34.5 billion for Chrome

rungs.purpose: Hook: a startup offers more than it is worth for the browser the viewer uses; the viewer wonders why, and whether it worked.

lines.text: Perplexity, an AI search startup, offered Google $34.5 billion in cash for Chrome, more than Perplexity itself was worth.

rungs.purpose: Set the stage: a judge is about to decide whether Google must sell Chrome, so the bid has a window.

lines.text: That August, Judge Amit Mehta was about to decide whether Google, already found to hold an illegal search monopoly, must sell Chrome.

rungs.purpose: Motive: what Srinivas wanted from Chrome and why, so the viewer understands the stakes for him.

lines.text: Perplexity's CEO, Aravind Srinivas, wanted Chrome's more than three billion users, and a way around browsers owned by his main rival, Google.

rungs.purpose: The move: the letter to Pichai, framed as the court's own fix; the viewer sees the bid is aimed at the judge.

lines.text: His letter to Google's CEO, Sundar Pichai, pitched the sale as the court's fix, "placing Chrome with a capable, independent operator."

rungs.purpose: The pressure: promises and a three-day deadline put the clock on Google.

lines.text: It promised to keep Google as Chrome's default search, and gave Google until August 15 to sign.
lines.must_show: Offer letter text with the signing deadline

rungs.purpose: The doubt begins: no named source for the money.

lines.text: Perplexity didn't say where the money would come from, beyond unnamed funds offering to cover it.

rungs.purpose: The gap: the price is far above Perplexity's own value, paying off the hook's 'more than it was worth'.

lines.text: Reuters said Perplexity was last valued at $14 billion, while other reports said $18 billion.

rungs.purpose: The contradiction: the bidder had publicly said Chrome should stay with Google; the viewer questions what the bid really was.

lines.text: Yet four months earlier, as Search Engine Journal reported, Srinivas had posted that "Chrome should remain within and continue to be run by Google."

rungs.purpose: Peak: the judge rules Google keeps Chrome, and the bid's window shuts.

lines.text: On September 2, Mehta ruled that Google would keep Chrome, calling a sale messy and risky for a browser built on Google's systems.

rungs.purpose: Landing: the $34.5 billion offer never even appears in the ruling, which answers whether the bid moved the court.

lines.text: And according to Courthouse News, his 230-page opinion never discusses Perplexity's $34.5 billion offer at all.

draft.close_question: Was Perplexity's Chrome bid ever serious?
